title: HTTP, REST & API Engineering
readme:
FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE
Volume 02 - Frontend + Backend Foundations
Phase 05 - HTTP, REST & API Engineering

This package contains 10 focused Phase 05 PDFs, one combined complete book, and a reference TaskFlow HTTP API snapshot.

Phase boundaries:
- Backend remains NestJS 12.0.3 + Fastify v5.
- Frontend and backend are still not connected.
- No CORS yet; it appears in Phase 06 when the browser actually calls the API.
- Todo data is intentionally in memory.
- No Prisma/PostgreSQL yet.
- No authentication yet.
- Manual input checks are educational scaffolding, not the later validation architecture.

Primary protocol references:
- RFC 9110 - HTTP Semantics, RFC Editor
- MDN HTTP Reference / HTTP Request Methods
- NestJS Controllers documentation

Next: Phase 06 - Next.js <-> NestJS Communication.

HTTP Mental Model
Client, server, resource, representation and contract

HTTP is the contract between independent programs.

REQUEST
HTTP Client                                                           TaskFlow API

PowerShell / browser / later Next.js                                            NestJS + Fastify
RESPONSE

method + target + headers + optional body

status + headers + optional body

Figure - HTTP request/response exchange. Phase 05 studies the protocol before Phase 06 introduces a browser cross-origin call.

Book 1 of Phase 05

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                                                HTTP Mental Model

HTTP is a contract, not a framework feature
NestJS did not invent GET, status 200 or JSON. Next.js will not invent them either. Both applications participate in an HTTP
contract defined independently of either framework. That separation is useful: if you later replace Next.js with a mobile app,
or NestJS with another backend, the HTTP concepts remain recognizable.

HTTP is the contract between independent programs.

REQUEST
HTTP Client                                                                  TaskFlow API

PowerShell / browser / later Next.js                                                   NestJS + Fastify
RESPONSE

method + target + headers + optional body

status + headers + optional body

Figure - HTTP request/response exchange. Phase 05 studies the protocol before Phase 06 introduces a browser cross-origin call.

The roles
Role                              Meaning in TaskFlow

Client                            A program that initiates a request. In this phase: PowerShell. Later: Next.js/browser.

Server                            The TaskFlow NestJS + Fastify process listening on port 4000.

Resource                          The thing addressed by the request, such as the Todo collection or a specific Todo.

Representation                    A transferable form of resource state, commonly JSON in our API.

Contract                          The agreed method, URL, headers, body shape, status and response shape.

One request has one primary direction
The client decides when to initiate an ordinary HTTP request. The server receives it, processes it, and sends a response. This
is different from realtime push architectures, which appear much later. Understanding ordinary request/response behavior
first makes later realtime technology easier to justify.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                                          HTTP Mental Model

Resource identity and request semantics are separate

Todo Collection

/todos

Todo 1                              Todo 2                              Todo 3

/todos/1                            /todos/2                            /todos/3

URLs identify resources. HTTP methods express what the client asks to do with them.

Figure - REST-oriented resource modeling separates resource identity from method semantics.

The URL identifies what the request targets. The HTTP method contributes what kind of operation the client is requesting.
This is why GET /todos/3 and DELETE /todos/3 can target the same resource while expressing different semantics.

Mental model

Think: resource + method + representation + outcome. Do not think: "controller function name somehow became an API."
The controller is only the server-side implementation of a protocol contract.

HTTP version vs HTTP semantics
HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 differ in framing, multiplexing and transport behavior. For application development, the
course first focuses on the shared semantics: methods, target URIs, fields/headers, representations and status codes. That
knowledge transfers across protocol versions.

What the server can and cannot infer
●    A server receives the request the client actually sent, not the request the developer intended to send.
●    If the path is wrong, routing may fail even if the JSON body is perfect.
●    If the method is wrong, the correct path may still not match the intended handler.
●    If JSON is malformed or the content type is incorrect, the server may not obtain the expected representation.
●    If a request succeeds but the status code is misleading, client code can still behave incorrectly.

REAL-WORLD NOTE

Mobile apps, CLI tools, partner integrations and browser frontends can all call the same HTTP API. A strong API contract
reduces coupling between those clients and the backend implementation.

Official source notes
Primary protocol reference: RFC 9110 - HTTP Semantics (RFC Editor). Supplemental developer reference: MDN HTTP Reference and
HTTP Request Methods. Nest-specific routing and status behavior reference: NestJS Controllers documentation.

HTTP Request and Response Anatomy
Methods, targets, headers, content, JSON and representations

HTTP is the contract between independent programs.

REQUEST
HTTP Client                                                           TaskFlow API

RESPONSE

method + target + headers + optional body

status + headers + optional body

Figure - HTTP request/response exchange. Phase 05 studies the protocol before Phase 06 introduces a browser cross-origin call.

Book 2 of Phase 05

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                           HTTP Request and Response Anatomy

Anatomy of an HTTP request

POST /todos HTTP/1.1

request line: method + target + protocol

Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
headers: metadata about the request

{"title":"Learn HTTP"}

body: representation sent to the server

Figure - Simplified HTTP request anatomy. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode messages differently on the wire, but the semantic concepts
remain method, target, headers and content.

Method
The method communicates the request semantics. GET asks for a representation; POST commonly submits content for
processing or creation; PUT requests replacement; PATCH requests a partial modification; DELETE requests removal.

Target
The request target identifies the addressed resource. In TaskFlow, /todos identifies the collection while /todos/3 identifies
one member. Query parameters can refine a request later, such as /todos?completed=true.

Headers
Header                                      Why it matters

Content-Type: application/json              Describes the media type of request content being sent.

Accept: application/json                    Expresses a representation preference for the response.

Authorization: Bearer ...                   Carries credentials later when authentication is introduced.

Cache-Control                               Influences caching behavior when relevant.

Body / content
A request may carry content. For a Todo creation request, JSON can represent the new data. GET normally retrieves data and
should not depend on a request body for ordinary API design.

JSON is a representation format, not HTTP itself
HTTP can carry many media types. TaskFlow uses JSON because it maps naturally to JavaScript data and is widely
supported. The protocol and the representation format remain separate concepts.
Example JSON representation

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                              HTTP Request and Response Anatomy

{
"title": "Learn HTTP",
"completed": false
}

Anatomy of an HTTP response

HTTP/1.1 201 Created

status line: protocol + status code + reason phrase

Content-Type: application/json
Location: /todos/3
response headers: metadata and controls

{"id":3,"title":"Learn HTTP","completed":false}

response body: selected representation

Figure - Simplified HTTP response anatomy. The status code is part of the contract, not decoration around JSON.

The status code summarizes the outcome at the protocol level. Headers provide metadata or controls. The response content
carries a representation when one is appropriate. A well-designed client uses all three instead of parsing a JSON message
string to guess whether the request succeeded.

Representation vs database row
Later, Prisma returns database records, but an API response does not have to expose a database row exactly as stored. A
representation is part of the API contract. This distinction becomes important when hiding internal fields, combining data or
versioning an API.

Boundary rule

Do not let the fact that JavaScript objects serialize easily to JSON trick you into thinking every internal object should
automatically become a public API response. Public representations are contracts.

VOLUME 02 - FRONTEND + BACKEND FOUNDATIONS

HTTP Methods, Status Codes and
Idempotency
Choose protocol semantics deliberately instead of by habit

HTTP is the contract between independent programs.

REQUEST
HTTP Client                                                           TaskFlow API

PowerShell / browser / later Next.js                                            NestJS + Fastify
RESPONSE

method + target + headers + optional body

status + headers + optional body

Figure - HTTP request/response exchange. Phase 05 studies the protocol before Phase 06 introduces a browser cross-origin call.

Book 3 of Phase 05

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                HTTP Methods, Status Codes and Idempotency

Method semantics matter

GET                           read                                safe + idempotent

POST                     create/action                         normally not idempotent

PUT                         replace                                  idempotent

PATCH                     partial change                      not guaranteed idempotent

DELETE                        remove                              idempotent semantics

Figure - Common method semantics. Safe and idempotent are protocol properties; they are not synonyms for "nothing happened" or
"same response".

RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as safe methods. Safe means the client is not requesting a
state-changing action. The server may still log the request or perform incidental work. Idempotent means multiple identical
requests have the same intended effect on the server as one request. Safe methods, PUT and DELETE are defined as
idempotent.

Safe is not the same as "zero side effects"
Logging a GET request changes a log file, but that does not make GET unsafe in HTTP semantics because the client did not
request that state change. The distinction is about the requested action.

Idempotent is not the same as "same response"
DELETE /todos/3 might return 204 the first time and 404 the second time. Those responses differ, yet the intended
resource-removal effect after repeated identical requests is still the same: Todo 3 is absent.

Common TaskFlow method choices
Operation                 Method             Route                             Reasoning

List Todos                GET                /todos                            Read collection representation.

Read Todo                 GET                /todos/:id                        Read one identified resource.

Create Todo               POST               /todos                            Server assigns a new member identity.

Replace Todo              PUT                /todos/:id                        Full replacement semantics; not used in our
first implementation.

Modify Todo               PATCH              /todos/:id                        Partial update of selected fields.

Delete Todo               DELETE             /todos/:id                        Request removal of identified resource.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                         HTTP Methods, Status Codes and Idempotency

Status code classes

1xx                      Information                               request processing / protocol info

2xx                       Success                                  request understood and handled

3xx                      Redirection                           further action or alternate representation

4xx            Client-side request problem                         request cannot be fulfilled as sent

5xx                  Server-side failure                  server failed while handling a valid-looking request

Figure - HTTP status codes are grouped by first digit. Application APIs mostly use 2xx, 4xx and 5xx in ordinary workflows.

Status codes used in this phase
Code                  Meaning in TaskFlow                                     Typical use

200 OK                Successful request with a response representation.      GET and PATCH here.

201 Created           A new resource was created.                             POST /todos.

204 No Content        Successful request intentionally returns no             DELETE /todos/:id.
response content.

400 Bad Request       Request cannot be processed as sent.                    Malformed/basic unusable input in examples.

404 Not Found         Target resource is not available.                       Unknown Todo id.

409 Conflict          Request conflicts with current resource/application     Later useful for uniqueness/state conflicts.
state.

500 Internal Server   Unexpected server failure.                              Do not intentionally use for client mistakes.
Error

Do not return 200 for everything

A response body such as {"success": false} with HTTP 200 forces every client to reinvent outcome detection. Use the protocol
status code accurately, then add structured error content when useful.

Book 4 of Phase 05

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                                 REST Resource and Route Design

Design APIs around resources

Todo Collection

/todos

Todo 1                              Todo 2                                Todo 3

/todos/1                            /todos/2                              /todos/3

URLs identify resources. HTTP methods express what the client asks to do with them.

Figure - REST-oriented resource modeling separates resource identity from method semantics.

REST is often taught as a rigid list of URL rules. A more useful starting point is resource-oriented thinking: identify the
domain concepts the client manipulates, give them stable resource identifiers, and use standard HTTP semantics to interact
with them.

Prefer nouns in resource paths
Avoid action-shaped route                                      Prefer resource-oriented route

GET /getTodos                                                  GET /todos

GET /getTodo?id=3                                              GET /todos/3

POST /createTodo                                               POST /todos

POST /completeTodo/3                                           PATCH /todos/3 with { completed: true }

POST /deleteTodo/3                                             DELETE /todos/3

This is not because verbs are forbidden in URLs. It is because HTTP already provides method semantics. Resource-oriented
contracts tend to be easier to predict and compose. Some domain actions genuinely do not map cleanly to CRUD; later
systems may use action endpoints when the domain warrants them.

Collections and members
Target                                 Examples of reasonable operations

/todos                                 GET list; POST create

/todos/:id                             GET one; PATCH change; DELETE remove

/projects/:projectId/tasks             Later: nested collection when project context is meaningful

Path parameters vs query parameters
Use path parameters to identify a resource or hierarchical context. Use query parameters to modify how a representation is
selected, filtered, sorted or paged.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                                  REST Resource and Route Design

Resource identity vs query refinement

GET /todos/42
GET /todos?completed=true
GET /todos?sort=createdAt&order=desc

Do not leak UI button names into the API
A frontend button might say Mark complete, but the API contract does not need a /markComplete route. The underlying
resource change is a Todo update. This keeps the API useful to clients that have completely different interfaces.

REAL-WORLD NOTE

A payroll or procurement API often includes operations that are more than CRUD, such as approve, post or close.
Resource-oriented design is a default mental model, not a command to distort domain workflows. Introduce explicit actions
when the domain operation is genuinely meaningful and cannot be represented clearly as ordinary resource state.

Contract checklist before implementing a route
●    What resource is being targeted?
●    Which HTTP method best expresses the requested semantics?
●    Where is resource identity carried: path or query?
●    Does the request need content? What media type?
●    What success status should the client expect?
●    What happens if the resource does not exist?
●    Is retrying the operation safe or idempotent?
●    What representation should a successful response expose?

Treat error responses as part of the API contract
Can the TCP request reach port 4000?
process + port

Did a route match?
method + path

Was the request representation usable?
headers + JSON shape

Did application logic succeed?
controller / service

What status and body came back?
observe exact response

Figure - HTTP debugging from the outside in. Preserve the request and response as evidence before editing code.

An API is not defined only by happy-path JSON. Clients must also know what happens when a route does not exist, a
resource is absent, the request content is unusable or the server fails unexpectedly.

404 can mean different things operationally
Observation                                        Likely meaning

404 for GET /todos/999                             Route matched; application says that resource does not exist.

404 for GET /todo/1                                Likely route mismatch: collection path is /todos.

404 for POST /todos/1 when no route exists         Method/path combination does not match a handler.

400 is for a request problem, not every business rejection
In this phase, a missing Todo title produces a basic 400 response. Later, formal DTO validation will give consistent
field-level errors. A state conflict such as creating a duplicate unique value may be better represented by 409. Status selection
should describe the kind of failure, not merely "something went wrong."

5xx means the server failed
Do not deliberately convert expected client mistakes into 500 responses. A 500-class response tells the client the server could
not fulfill the request because of a server-side failure. Production systems should log the internal details without leaking
secrets or stack traces into public responses.

Inspect what you actually sent
1      Record the exact method.
2      Record the exact URL, including port and query string.
3      Record request headers that affect representation, especially Content-Type.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                                  HTTP Error Semantics and Debugging

4       Record the JSON content exactly as serialized.
5       Observe the numeric status code.
6       Observe response headers and body.
7       Only then decide which application layer to inspect.

A useful debugging contrast
PowerShell

# Wrong path
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Get -Uri 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/todo/1'

# Correct path
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Get -Uri 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/todos/1'

If the first request returns 404, editing TodosService would be irrational: the route may never have reached the service.
Debugging improves when you trace from observable protocol evidence inward.

Error-driven teaching rule

Preserve the failing request. Form one hypothesis. Change the smallest relevant thing. Repeat the same request. If the symptom
changes, you learned something about the layer.

Book 8 of Phase 05

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                         API Design Decisions and Anti-Patterns

API design decisions that age well
Decision                    Prefer                                         Avoid

Resource naming             Plural nouns such as /todos                    Verb-heavy routes such as /getTodos

Outcome signaling           Meaningful HTTP status                         Always 200 + success boolean

Representation              Stable public shape                            Blindly expose every internal object

Deletion                    DELETE /todos/:id                              POST /deleteTodo

Partial edit                PATCH /todos/:id                               One endpoint per field/button

Errors                      Consistent status + structured body            Random strings and stack traces

Testing                     Independent API client first                   Only test through UI clicks

Anti-pattern: controller as the entire application
The controller should not gradually accumulate arrays, database queries, permission rules and business workflows. Phase 05
keeps the in-memory array in TodosService so that when persistence changes later, the HTTP boundary remains conceptually
stable.

Anti-pattern: status code as decoration
If a client must inspect { success: false } to discover that a request failed while the HTTP status is 200, intermediaries,
monitoring tools and generic client behavior lose useful protocol information. Use HTTP semantics rather than hiding them
inside JSON.

Anti-pattern: design from screens instead of domain
resources
A UI might have buttons named Add, Finish, Archive, Restore and Delete. If every button becomes an endpoint name, the
API becomes tightly coupled to one interface. Start from the resource and its state transitions, then introduce explicit action
endpoints only when the domain operation itself deserves an action concept.

Anti-pattern: pretending Phase 05 input handling is
production validation
The manual title check in POST /todos is intentionally minimal. It does not give reusable schemas, transformation,
field-specific validation or consistent DTO behavior. Later phases introduce a real validation boundary. A professional
course should label temporary scaffolding honestly.

API contract review checklist
●     Is the resource name meaningful without seeing the frontend?
●     Does the method match the intended semantics?
●     Can a client predict common success and failure statuses?
●     Is the response shape stable and intentional?
●     Is resource identity in the correct part of the URL?
●     Are query parameters used for selection/filter/sort rather than hidden actions?
●     Is the endpoint independently testable?

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 05                                                              API Design Decisions and Anti-Patterns

●    If the UI disappeared tomorrow, would the API still make sense?

Architecture before abstraction

We still do not add repository interfaces, shared API packages or OpenAPI generators. The learner first needs a real contract
worth abstracting. Later phases can introduce tooling when a concrete maintenance problem appears.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 05: HTTP, REST & API Engineering

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
Client intent -> HTTP method + URI -> headers/body -> server processing -> status + response representation -> client state transition

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Using 200 for every outcome
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Encoding actions into routes when resource semantics are clearer
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Returning database rows as accidental public contracts
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Confusing authentication failures with authorization failures
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — HTTP, REST & API Engineering

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 05 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Design HTTP APIs using resources, methods, status codes, idempotency, errors, caching semantics, and versionable contracts.

Required artifact
A written TaskFlow API contract for tasks with request/response examples and deliberate error semantics.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can design a resource-oriented route set.
• Can choose meaningful status codes.
• Can explain idempotency.
• Can reason about API contract evolution.

Independent build sequence
1. Write the task resource shape before writing controller code.
2. Design collection and item URIs and justify GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE choices.
3. Define success and failure status codes for create, read, update, delete, validation, auth, forbidden, and missing-resource cases.
4. Use curl or an API client to inspect raw headers and bodies rather than only frontend behavior.
5. Repeat safe/idempotent requests and reason about what should or should not change.
6. Write an error envelope that the frontend can parse consistently.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Mastery Capstone Lab

Evidence packet
